headings.title: Introduction to Sample Design in Nursing Research
headings.content: Sample design is a foundational concept in nursing research, serving as the blueprint for how researchers select a subset of individuals to participate in a study. In clinical nursing, it is rarely feasible, cost-effective, or ethical to study an entire population of patients, such as every individual living with type 2 diabetes in Nigeria. Instead, nurse researchers rely on sample design to select a representative group that reflects the characteristics of the larger target population. A well-designed sample ensures that the findings of a research study can be generalized with confidence, enhancing the validity and applicability of evidence-based nursing interventions. Without a rigorous sample design, research outcomes may be skewed, leading to incorrect clinical guidelines and compromised patient care. Nursing students must understand that the choice of sample design directly dictates the strength of evidence generated, influencing everything from local hospital protocols to national health policies. Whether exploring the efficacy of a new wound care dressing or assessing maternal mortality risk factors, the integrity of the research begins with a thoughtful and deliberate sampling strategy. By mastering sample design, future nurses develop the critical appraisal skills necessary to evaluate published literature and integrate valid scientific findings into their daily clinical practice.

headings.title: Key Terminology: Population, Sample, and Sampling Frame
headings.content: To understand sample design, nursing students must master three fundamental statistical terms: population, sample, and sampling frame. The target population refers to the entire aggregate of cases or individuals that meet the specific criteria defined by the researcher, such as all registered nurses working in tertiary hospitals in Lagos State. Because studying the entire target population is impractical, researchers select a sample, which is the specific subset of individuals from the population who actually participate in the study. Bridging the gap between the target population and the sample is the sampling frame. The sampling frame is the actual, concrete list or operationalized roster of all elements or members of the population from which the sample is drawn. For example, if a researcher wants to study nursing students at a specific university, the registrar's official enrollment list serves as the sampling frame. Discrepancies between the target population and the sampling frame can introduce coverage error. If the sampling frame excludes certain groups, such as distance-learning students, the resulting sample will not truly represent the broader population. Recognizing these distinctions enables nurse researchers to critically appraise whether a study's sample accurately reflects the population it claims to represent.

headings.title: Probability Sampling Methods
headings.content: Probability sampling methods are characterized by the randomized selection of subjects, ensuring that every individual in the sampling frame has a known, non-zero probability of being chosen. This approach is the gold standard in quantitative nursing research because it minimizes selection bias and allows researchers to calculate sampling error statistically, thereby maximizing generalizability. Simple random sampling is the most basic form, where every member has an equal chance of selection, often achieved using a table of random numbers or computer software. Systematic sampling involves selecting every 'k-th' individual from a ordered list, starting from a randomly determined point. Stratified random sampling divides the population into homogeneous subgroups, or strata—such as male and female nurses, or nurses across different wards—and then randomly selects participants from each stratum in proportion to their actual population size. This ensures that minority or crucial subgroups are adequately represented. Cluster sampling involves dividing the population into naturally occurring groups, such as hospitals or primary health care clinics, and randomly selecting entire clusters for study. While probability sampling requires a comprehensive sampling frame and can be logistically challenging in resource-limited clinical settings, its scientific rigor makes it exceptionally valuable for establishing broad epidemiological and clinical facts.

headings.title: Non-Probability Sampling Methods in Clinical Studies
headings.content: Non-probability sampling methods involve non-random selection processes where not every member of the population has a known chance of being included. In many clinical nursing studies, practical constraints such as time, budget, and the difficulty of accessing specific patient groups make probability sampling impossible. Consequently, non-probability methods are widely utilized, particularly in qualitative research, pilot studies, and exploratory clinical evaluations. Convenience sampling is the most common technique, relying on participants who are readily available and meet the inclusion criteria, such as patients attending an outpatient clinic on a specific morning. While convenient and inexpensive, it carries a high risk of selection bias and limits the ability to generalize findings. Quota sampling is an enhancement of convenience sampling, where the researcher ensures specific proportions of demographic groups are included, mirroring population characteristics. Purposive or judgmental sampling involves selecting participants based on the researcher's expert knowledge of who can provide the best information, commonly used in qualitative nursing studies to explore lived experiences. Snowball sampling, or network sampling, relies on initial participants to refer other eligible subjects, which is particularly useful for hard-to-reach or stigmatized populations, such as intravenous drug users or patients with rare infectious diseases. Although non-probability samples lack statistical generalizability, they provide rich, contextual insights crucial for advancing nursing knowledge.

headings.title: Determining Sample Size and Power
headings.content: Determining the appropriate sample size is a critical step in research design that directly impacts the validity and reliability of study findings. If a sample is too small, the study may lack statistical power, resulting in a Type II error—failing to detect a real clinical effect or treatment difference that actually exists. Conversely, an unnecessarily large sample wastes financial and human resources and can expose more participants than necessary to clinical trial burdens. Calculating sample size requires understanding four key parameters: effect size, level of significance (alpha), statistical power, and the variance within the data. Effect size measures the magnitude of the difference or relationship being studied; a smaller effect size requires a larger sample to detect. Alpha, typically set at 0.05, represents the acceptable probability of committing a Type I error (finding a false positive). Statistical power is conventionally set at 0.80 or 80%, representing the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis. Nursing researchers use specialized software formulas, power tables, or expert statisticians to compute the minimum required sample size before data collection begins. For survey-based or clinical nursing studies, researchers must also factor in anticipated attrition or dropout rates, inflating the initial sample size to ensure that an adequate number of completed responses remains at the study's conclusion.

headings.title: Addressing Sampling Bias and Error
headings.content: Sampling bias and sampling error are two distinct challenges that can severely compromise the integrity of nursing research. Sampling error is the natural variation that occurs when data is collected from a sample rather than the entire population; it is a random discrepancy that decreases as sample size increases and can be estimated statistically. In contrast, sampling bias is a systematic error introduced when the selection process favors certain individuals over others, resulting in a sample that is unrepresentative of the target population. Bias can stem from various sources, including flawed sampling frames, volunteer bias (where individuals who volunteer have different health behaviors than non-volunteers), and non-response bias (where patients who drop out or refuse to participate share specific characteristics). For instance, if a nurse researcher studies patient satisfaction but only surveys patients who are discharged during morning shifts, evening and night-shift patients are excluded, introducing systematic bias. To mitigate these issues, nurse researchers must employ rigorous randomization techniques, maximize response rates through clear communication and incentives, compare characteristics of responders versus non-responders, and explicitly acknowledge limitations in their published work. Recognizing and controlling for bias ensures that nursing evidence remains objective, trustworthy, and clinically applicable.

headings.title: Ethical Considerations in Sample Recruitment
headings.content: Ethical considerations are paramount during sample recruitment in clinical nursing research. Because research involving human subjects carries inherent vulnerabilities, particularly when patients are ill or hospitalized, strict ethical principles must guide every stage of participant selection. The fundamental principles of autonomy, beneficence, and justice must be upheld. Autonomy is operationalized through voluntary informed consent, ensuring that patients understand they have the right to participate or refuse participation without fear of compromising their standard healthcare services. Coercion or undue influence—such as offering excessive financial incentives to impoverished patients or implying that treatment depends on research participation—is strictly unethical. Beneficence requires researchers to maximize potential benefits while minimizing physical, psychological, or social risks to participants. Justice mandates fair and equitable selection of samples, preventing researchers from unfairly burdening marginalized groups, such as low-income patients or prisoners, simply because they are easily accessible. Furthermore, nurse researchers must protect patient privacy and confidentiality by anonymizing or de-identifying data collected from the sample. Institutional Review Board (IRB) or ethical committee approval must be secured prior to approaching any potential participants, ensuring that the proposed sample design respects human dignity and adheres to international and national research ethics guidelines.
